title:
Firm divisionalization and the gender gap in
                    <scp>CEO</scp>
                    promotion
affiliations: Management, Human Resources, and Information Systems Academic Area, Orfalea College of Business California Polytechnic State University San Luis Obispo California USA; Management Department, Isenberg School of Management University of Massachusetts Amherst Amherst Massachusetts USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This study examines how divisionalized firm structures shape the gender gap in internal chief executive officer (CEO) promotion. We argue that divisionalized firms may narrow the gender gap in CEO succession by generating more individually attributable performance information about senior managers. In contrast to firms in which candidates' contributions are difficult to isolate, divisionalized firms create profit‐and‐loss (P&L) accountability that makes managerial performance more visible and comparable. Using longitudinal data on over 616,000 managers in 49,135 US firms, we find that women are more likely to be promoted to CEO in divisionalized firms. We also find that the gender gap is smaller among managers with prior P&L‐accountable experience. Among managers in divisionalized firms, stronger unit performance relative to within‐firm peers is more positively associated with promotion to CEO for women than for men. The results highlight organizational structure as a potential source of variation in gender inequality in executive advancement. Managerial Summary Why do so few women become CEOs? Part of the answer lies in how firms are organized. When a company is structured into divisions with their own profit‐and‐loss responsibility, the results of the managers who lead those units are easier to observe, compare, and credit to the individual. This leaves less room for subjective judgments through which gender bias often enters promotion decisions. In data on more than 600,000 managers at roughly 49,000 US firms, we find that women are more likely to be promoted to CEO in divisionalized firms. The pattern is strongest for women who have led a business unit, and strong unit results count for more in women's promotion prospects. For boards seeking greater gender equity in CEO succession, structures and evaluation systems that give senior leaders clear, comparable performance records may matter as much as diversity initiatives.

title: Organizational Consolidation: How Organizations Reflect or Refract Societal Hierarchies
affiliations: Rutgers University
abstract: To understand how organizations distribute resources, we need to understand how they come to evaluate their members as worthy. This article introduces “organizational consolidation”: the degree to which ascriptive statuses—race, gender, class—align with the context-specific criteria that actors use when evaluating one another. Building on relational inequality theory and inhabited institutionalism, we argue that organizational consolidation shapes which attributes stand out, how actors categorize one another, and how combinations of attributes yield recognition or marginalization. When consolidation is high, local meaning-making is more likely to reproduce patterns of recognition that track ascriptive statuses; when it is low, alternative patterns become possible. We develop a concept-methods package that turns this framework into a roadmap for observing local patterns of recognition: association rule mining, latent class analysis, and partial order set modeling. We illustrate the value of these tools in a small, racially diverse U.S. high school where consolidation is low: teachers evaluate students through combinations of race, gender, and organizationally relevant characteristics, rather than any single attribute. By formalizing organizational consolidation as a measurable structural condition, we provide a diagnostic for comparing how organizations reflect or refract broader social hierarchies—shifting focus to how and under what organizational conditions inequality takes the specific forms it does.

title: Prophet Inequalities for a New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping
authors: Jacob Feldman; Yukai Huang; Panos Kouvelis
affiliations: Olin Business School, Washington University, Saint Louis, Missouri 63130; Sawyer Business School, Suffolk University, Boston, Massachusetts 02108
abstract: A New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping Industry Container carriers lose billions of dollars each year when shippers reserve slots but fail to show up with the corresponding cargo. This paper studies an online booking problem under a deposit-based mechanism designed to better align incentives and mitigate the costs of overbooking. The authors derive near-optimal online policies for two demand settings: one in which shippers’ no-show behavior is coupled through a spot market, and another in which no-shows are independent. In the coupled setting, a randomized threshold policy guarantees at least 81.9% of clairvoyant profit. In the independent setting, a simple greedy policy is shown to be asymptotically 0.5-optimal as the number of slots tends to infinity. Extensive simulations further demonstrate strong and robust practical performance.

title: Beyond Value: On the Role of Symmetry in Demand for Information
authors: Aniol Llorente-Saguer; Santiago Oliveros; Ro’i Zultan
affiliations: School of Economics and Finance, Queen Mary University of London, London E1 4NS, United Kingdom; Department of Economics, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TU, United Kingdom; Department of Economics, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Beer-Sheva 8410501, Israel
abstract: We study demand for symmetric and asymmetric information sources in the laboratory. Although participants respond to incentives and instrumental considerations, they exhibit a systematic bias towards symmetric sources. These patterns persist among individuals with higher cognitive abilities and better task comprehension, and they are not accounted for by their elicited subjective beliefs. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioural economics and decision analysis. Funding: This project was supported by a British Academy/Leverhulme Small Research [Grant SG171679]. R. title: The impact of migration and institutions on new business creation: integrating social capital theory and institutional theory
authors: Dekuwmini Mornah; Raymond MacDermott; Felicia Naatu
abstract: Abstract Migration and remittances now shape entrepreneurial ecosystems across the developing world, yet their effects remain contradictory: financial remittances sometimes spur new ventures and sometimes suppress them, and emigrant stocks produce inconsistent outcomes across contexts. We help to resolve this puzzle by theorizing nonlinear relationships and institutional contingencies. Drawing on transnational social capital theory and institutional theory, we introduce Social Connectivity Capacity (SCC), the structural capacity of transnational networks to transmit entrepreneurially relevant knowledge, operationalized as the product of emigrant stocks and internet penetration. Panel analyses of 85 migrant-sending countries (2006–2020) show that financial remittances exhibit a convex, accelerating relationship with new business creation, while SCC follows an inverted U-shape. Formal institutional quality moderates both relationships: stronger governance amplifies remittance-driven entrepreneurship and shifts SCC's optimum rightward. Results are robust across GLS and panel-corrected-SE estimators and to log-transformation. These findings account for prior mixed evidence and show that migration's entrepreneurial effects depend jointly on remittance intensity, digital connectivity, and institutional context. Policymakers in migrant-sending countries can therefore strengthen entrepreneurial outcomes by calibrating diaspora engagement strategies to their specific combination of remittance intensity, digital infrastructure, and governance quality.

title: The historical evolution of international business: growth trajectory of an academic field of study
The innovation tug‐of‐war: Local grit versus global grit in emerging markets
affiliations: Norwich Business School University of East Anglia Norwich UK; Birmingham Business School University of Birmingham Birmingham UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Drawing on vicarious learning, competition‐driven innovation incentives, and the temporal dynamics of competitive activity, this study explores which type of competition, local versus foreign, most benefits advanced economy MNEs' (AEMNEs) emerging market (EM) innovation performance, when and in what temporal patterns. We predict that local competition contributes more to AEMNEs' EM innovation performance and that this positive impact is reinforced by foreign competition. We further predict that irregular local competition amplifies the innovation performance‐enhancing effect of local competition, whereas irregular foreign competition diminishes the benefits of foreign competition for innovation performance. Our multi‐level analysis of AEMNEs operating in China's high‐tech sector supports these predictions. The findings offer novel insights into how competition heterogeneity and its temporal dynamics shape the innovation performance of AEMNEs in EMs. Managerial Summary AEMNEs face competition from both local and foreign rivals, but not all competition equally drives innovation. Our study of AEMNEs operating in China shows that competing with local counterparts delivers greater innovation performance, and the innovation benefits of engaging with one type of rival are reinforced by the other. Competitive rhythm also matters. Local competition enhances innovation when local rivals act irregularly, while irregular moves by foreign peers reduce their innovation benefits. Managers should strategically track both competitor types and align innovation efforts with the rhythm of market dynamics to maximize innovation outcomes.

title: Issue Information
Probabilistic Assessment of the Relative Source Contribution Factor While Accounting for Exposure to Other Regulated Media: A Toxicokinetic Proof‐of‐Concept for Volatile Drinking Water Contaminants
affiliations: Direction de la santé environnementale, au travail et de la toxicologie Institut national de santé publique du Québec (INSPQ) Montréal Québec Canada; Département de santé environnementale et santé au travail École de santé publique de l'Université de Montréal (ESPUM) Montréal Québec Canada
abstract: ABSTRACT A relative source contribution factor is applied when deriving noncancer health‐based guidance values for drinking water contaminants. The present work aimed at assessing the adequacy of the 20% default value often attributed to this factor while accounting for concomitant inhalation exposure to the reference concentration (RfC). Steady‐state toxicokinetic equations were applied to calculate constant blood concentration (Cblood ss ) in adults and 1–3‐year‐old children for 12 volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Three exposure scenarios were considered for each compound, namely, (1) ingestion of the reference dose (RfD) alone; (2) inhalation of the RfC alone; and (3) ingestion of 20% of the RfD combined with inhalation of the RfC. Using Monte Carlo simulations, probabilistic ratios of Cblood ss were computed for Scenario 3 over Scenario 1. Ratios >1, demonstrating an exceedance of the RfD‐equivalent Cblood ss by Scenario 3, are obtained at mean and 97.5 th percentile value for eight of the chosen VOCs in adults, with range of 0.3–29 at the mean and of 0.32–52 at the 97.5 th percentile. Nine VOCs exhibited such exceedance in children (ranges: 0.34–36 at the mean; 0.38–57 at the 97.5 th percentile). For eight VOCs, ratios >1 were mainly explained by high RfC‐related intake as compared to RfD‐related intake. Concluding, steady‐state toxicokinetic modeling was successfully used to illustrate the importance of other media's guidance levels‐related exposures, in the present case the RfC, to evaluate the magnitude of the relative source contribution factor required when determining health‐based guidance values for chemicals in drinking water.

title: Two Foundational Ideas of Risk—Undesirability and Unexpectedness—With Implications for Risk Science and Its Applications
affiliations: University of Stavanger Stavanger Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper contends that the concept of risk is fundamentally shaped by two distinct motivating ideas: (1) that something undesirable may occur (dominant in safety, security, and engineering contexts), and (2) that something unexpected may occur (central to many business, strategic, and decision‐making domains). Any framework aspiring to generality across diverse application areas must therefore be sufficiently inclusive to accommodate both perspectives. The paper explores the ramifications of this dual conceptualization for foundational aspects of risk science—including core definitions, the scope and boundaries of the discipline—as well as for risk understanding, communication, and management.

title: Research on Risk Classification of Online Public Opinion in Emergencies Based on FHCO Algorithm
affiliations: School of Economics and Management Southwest Petroleum University Chengdu China
abstract: ABSTRACT Online public opinion concerning emergencies presents challenges to social stability due to its rapid dissemination and complex evolutionary nature. Accurate risk classification is essential for effective early warning. Current risk classification methods, however, face limitations such as difficulty in capturing complex structural features at a single scale, inadequate representation of local risk variations, and imprecision in threshold determination. To address these issues, this article proposes a risk classification method on the basis of the fractal hierarchical clustering optimization (FHCO) algorithm for public risk perception and discursive reflection. First, a comprehensive set of risk indicators for online public opinion is constructed. Next, fractal characteristics—including the correlation function, generalized dimension spectrum, singularity index, and fractal spectrum—are calculated. These fractal features are then clustered using the FHCO algorithm, and the final risk level is determined by integrating the comprehensive risk score. To validate the method's effectiveness, the “7.20” Zhengzhou rainstorm incident was analyzed as a case study, along with 27 other high‐risk public opinion events. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 92.86%, significantly outperforming the traditional K ‐means (64.29%) and K ‐medoids (82.14%) algorithms. This demonstrates that the method can effectively improve the accuracy of risk classification, providing new insights and technical support for the early identification of online public opinion risks associated with emergencies.

title: The Right Key for the Right Lock: How Government Response Methods and Demand Types Affect Citizen Satisfaction
authors: Na Tang; Wenjia Huang; Nana Huang; Mengyao Zhang
affiliations: College of Public Administration, Huazhong University of Science and Technology Wuhan China
abstract: ABSTRACT Faced with diverse and complex demands from citizens, the government has consistently sought ways to enhance its ability to respond. Metaphorically, citizens' needs can be viewed as locks, and the government requires keys to unlock them. Artificial intelligence (AI) is an innovative new key offering a fresh paradigm for unlocking the door to high citizen satisfaction. Drawing on government responsiveness theory, this study applies a 2 × 3 between‐subjects survey experiment to explore the impact of government response methods (traditional responses, AI‐enabled responses) and citizen demand types (consultation, complaint/help‐seeking, suggestions) on citizen satisfaction. Findings show that AI‐enabled government responses significantly increase citizen satisfaction compared to traditional approaches. Among demand types, consultation yields the highest satisfaction, while suggestion results in the lowest. Further, the satisfaction level is significantly influenced by the interaction effect between response method and demand type. Perceived fairness mediates the relationship between government responses and citizen satisfaction, with citizen participation experience having a moderating effect. This study offers new insights into increasing citizen satisfaction from the perspective of government responses. It reveals the content‐dependent nature of AI‐enabled government responses, helping the government create unique AI response strategies and enhance digital interaction with citizens.

title: Labor Market Frictions and Product Differentiation: Evidence From Salary History Bans
affiliations: King's Business School King's College London London UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Salary History Bans (SHBs) prohibit employers from requesting applicants' salary histories, shifting bargaining power toward workers and reducing employers' information about worker productivity. We find that SHB adoption is associated with lower product differentiation, particularly among firms with greater exposure to labor costs and innovative investment, greater reliance on skilled labor and exposure to hiring frictions, and rents not already contested through collective bargaining. These findings support both bargaining and information asymmetry channels. SHBs are also associated with lower operating margins among highly differentiated firms, suggesting that weaker differentiation ultimately erodes the product‐market performance of industry leaders.
journal: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: What Future for Genetics in Management Research?
affiliations: Villanova University
abstract: Abstract The author teams on this Point‐Counterpoint debate agree that the search for genetic explanations of organizational behaviours has been underwhelming – yet they have very different visions for the future of genetics in management research. The Point argues for a deeper dive into the field of genetics to ensure more precise measurement and make better causal inferences. In contrast, the Counterpoint cautions against reducing complex human behaviour to molecular causes and sees genetics as better suited to explain distal evolutionary conditions from which behaviours emerge. The introduction to this collection summarizes the core ideas in each article and their recommendations. The introduction then positions the Point‐Counterpoint debate against the broader challenge of seeking to advance management research with knowledge from a different discipline. It concludes with a call for researchers to carefully consider when and under what conditions it is warranted to search for genetic explanations, rather than uncritically embracing genetic explanations or dismissing them outright.

title: From Micro to Macro in an Equilibrium Diffusion Model
authors: Wyatt Brooks; Kevin Donovan; Terence R. Johnson
affiliations: Arizona State University; Yale University and NBER; University of Virginia
abstract: Abstract We quantify the benefits of better firm-to-firm matching in an aggregate diffusion model where individuals acquire profitable knowledge from others. We estimate the model using a small-scale program in Kenya that creates new opportunities for firm managers to interact. Aggregate gains from the program depend on the relative importance of meeting a high-knowledge firm versus learning within that meeting. We show how moments from the intervention identify these parameters, demonstrating how easily estimated moments beyond the average treatment effect inform at-scale gains. We provide sufficient conditions extending the identification procedure to a broader class of experiments and aggregate diffusion models.

title: Transaction Costs and the Gains from Trade in Water Markets
affiliations: Montana State University nicholas.hagerty@montana.edu
abstract: Abstract Surface water in California is scarce and tightly managed, yet little is traded through a market. This paper studies transaction costs in the existing wholesale water market and estimates the benefits of reducing them. I develop an empirical framework that uses transactions among water districts to analyze welfare, decomposing prices into demand and transaction costs and simulating a market with only physical frictions. Transaction costs are large: median variable costs are 54% of the price, and fixed costs deter many districts from participating. Eliminating them produces gains of several hundred million dollars per year, or 1-3% of statewide water expenditures.

title: Insurance Choice with Non-Monetary Plan Attributes: Limited Consideration in Medicare Part D
affiliations: Rice University
abstract: Abstract I propose a model of insurance demand where non-monetary attributes determine which plans an individual considers, and monetary attributes determine an individual's expected utility. This approach reconciles the classic view of insurance as purely financial with the empirical finding that choice is driven by additional attributes. I estimate the model using Medicare Part D data, allowing for unobserved heterogeneity in consideration and preferences. I find the former plays a crucial role: more than 90% of individuals consider 5 or fewer plans, approximately lO°lo of the menu. Additionally, estimates of risk preferences are comparable to existing studies of similar stakes.

title: Social Ties and Fiscal Transfers in a Regional Economy: A Quantitative Spatial Analysis
authors: Yuwan Duan; Yatang Lin; Yi Lu
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Tsinghua University
abstract: Abstract Many governments use fiscal transfers to reduce regional inequality, yet discretionary allocation may also depend on informal communication among officials. We examine this mechanism in a large central-to-provincial transfer system, using policymakers’ shared workplace, alumni, and hometown backgrounds to measure social ties. Exploiting ministerial turnover and controlling for provincial leadership, we find that prior workplace ties significantly increase transfers. We then embed these estimates in a quantitative spatial model with trade, migration, input-output linkages, and fiscal-productivity effects. Social ties redirect resources toward richer provinces with stronger fundamentals, raising welfare and output while weakening redistribution. Under egalitarian weights, however, removing ties improves welfare.

title: Scientific Talent Leaks Out of Funding Gaps
authors: Wei Yang Tham; Joseph Staudt; Elisabeth Ruth Perlman; Stephanie D. Cheng
affiliations: University of Toronto weiyang.tham@rotman.utoronto.ca; US Census Bureau joseph.staudt@census.gov; US Census Bureau elisabeth.perlman@census.gov; Analysis Group
abstract: Abstract Federal research funding is a key input into scientific work, but funding streams can be disrupted. We study how delays in renewed NIH research grants affect lab personnel’s careers, linking grant records to university payroll, tax, Census, and publication data. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that interruptions of at least 30 days increase nonemployment among personnel in labs supported by a single NIH R01 grant by 3 percentage points, or 40%. Among those who remain employed in the US, earnings decrease by 20%. The results show that short funding gaps can alter career trajectories, especially for trainees.

title: Return to Office and the Tenure Distribution
authors: David Van Dijcke; Florian Gunsilius; Austin Wright
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Virginia; Department of Economics, Emory University; Harris School of Public Policy, University of Chicago
abstract: Abstract Debates over return-to-office mandates have intensified since the COVID-19 pandemic ended, though their economic implications remain poorly understood. Using large-scale resume data, we analyze how these policies affect employee tenure and seniority at three large U.S. tech companies: Microsoft, SpaceX, and Apple. Employing a distributional synthetic controls framework, we estimate a reduction in tenure and seniority at firms returning to the office. We extend the framework with a functional bootstrap procedure and prove its validity for constructing uniform confidence bands. Return-to-office mandates appear to drive senior employees away, posing a risk to firm productivity and innovation.

title: Job Loss, Unemployment Insurance, and Health: Evidence from Brazil
authors: Guilherme Amorim; Diogo G. C. Britto; Alexandre Fonseca; Breno Sampaio
affiliations: University of Georgia amorim@uga.edu; Bocconi University, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), Prospera Lab, CEPR, IZA, IGIER diogo.britto@unibocconi.it; Federal Revenue of Brazil, Prospera Lab, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), GAPPE/UFPE alexandre.fonseca@rfb.gov.br; Federal University of Pernambuco, Prospera Lab, CLEAN Unit for the Economic Analysis of Crime (INSPIRE/Bocconi), GAPPE/UFPE brenorsampaio@gmail.com
abstract: Abstract We study the health impacts of job loss and unemployment insurance (UI) among Brazilian workers, using unique administrative data linking employment, hospitalizations, health insurance, and mortality records over 17 years. Leveraging mass layoffs for identification, we find that job loss raises hospitalization (+33%) and mortality (+23%) risks for men, with no significant effects for women. Impacts are pervasive across age, income, and education levels, with children of male workers also affected. External causes related to risky behavior and violence victimization explain half the effects. Using a regression discontinuity design, we show that UI partially mitigates health risks, suggesting that these are partially explained by income losses.

title: Estimating the Macroeconomic Effects of Oil Supply News
affiliations: Bank of Italy; Ghent University
abstract: Abstract We show that structural oil-market shocks identified in prominent SVAR models, as well as high-frequency oil price changes around OPEC announcements, are predictable, indicating informational deficiencies in standard oil-market VARs and contamination of commonly used instrumental variables. We resolve these identification problems for oil supply news shocks by augmenting the econometrician’s information set with financial indicators, yielding markedly different results: the shocks induce a sharper short-run output contraction, are less inflationary, contribute less to oil price variation, exhibit greater stability over time, and account for a substantial share of S&P 500 volatility.

title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Employers and the Earnings of Young Workers
affiliations: Opportunity Insights and Harvard University mstaiger@g.harvard.edu
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how parental connections to firms shape early-career earnings. I use employer-employee linked data to study one important type of connection: jobs obtained at a parent’s employer. Twenty-nine percent of individuals work for a parent’s employer at least once by age 30. Exploiting transitory, firm-specific fluctuations in hiring conditions at the parent’s employer, I estimate that working for a parent’s employer increases initial earnings by 24 percent, primarily by providing access to higher-paying firms. Individuals with higher-earning parents are more likely to work for a parent’s employer and experience larger earnings gains when they do. Consequently, the elasticity of initial earnings with respect to parental earnings would be 12 percent lower if no one found a job through these connections. The findings suggest that connections to firms through one’s social network may be an important determinant of intergenerational mobility.

title: Gender and Electoral Incentives: Evidence from COVID-19 Response
affiliations: Inter-American Development Bank juancha@iadb.org; UCLA Anderson and NBER clemence.tricaud@anderson.ucla.edu
abstract: Abstract This paper provides new evidence on why men and women leaders make different choices. Exploiting Brazilian close elections, we show that female mayors responded differently to the COVID-19 crisis over the year 2020. Female mayors were less likely to close non-essential businesses early in the pandemic and female-led municipalities experienced higher mortality, while the reverse was true later on. We show that these findings can be rationalized by a simple political agency model in which politicians seek re-election and voters are gender biased. Consistent with this interpretation, the gender differences we find are driven exclusively by mayors facing re-election.

title: Losing Political Representation
authors: Timo Wochner; Aaron Günther; Niklas Potrafke; Felix Rösel
affiliations: ETH Zurich; KOF Institute; CESifo, Munich; University of Munich (LMU); ifo Institute, Munich; TU Braunschweig
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of losing political representation in a democracy? A reform of Germany’s mixed electoral system left more than 7 million citizens in 23 constituencies without a directly elected representative after the 2025 national election. Which and how many constituencies were affected was unpredictable and quasi-random. We show that losing geographical representation reduces citizens’ satisfaction with democracy. Moreover, discontent is independent of party preferences and spreads through social networks, reducing democratic satisfaction even among individuals who were unaffected or unaware of the reform’s outcome. We conclude that political representation is a cornerstone of democracy.

title: Gender Discrimination in Access to Capital: A Field Experiment in Ethiopia
authors: Ketki Sheth; Shanthi Manian; Shibiru Ayalew
affiliations: University of Tennessee, Knoxville ksheth2@utk.edu; Washington State University shanthi@manian.org; Adama Science and Technology University, Ethiopia shibekoo84@gmail.com
abstract: Abstract We test whether loan officers discriminate against female business owners in capital decisions affecting real businesses in an Ethiopian business plan competition. Randomizing owner gender across 3,696 evaluations, by 84 loan officers, for 916 businesses, we find no effect on prize scores or consideration for a loan. Incentivized beliefs about future performance did not differ by gender, ruling out statistical and taste-based discrimination. Machine learning predictions of future business performance show that loan officers beliefs were accurate. Gender does not meaningfully improve predictions, implying no trade-off between gender equity and effective capital allocation.

title: Intergroup Contact, Empathy Education, and Refugee-Native Integration in Lebanon
authors: Salma Mousa; Lennard Naumann; Alexandra Scacco
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles; WZB Berlin Social Science Center; Humboldt University of Berlin; University of Hamburg
abstract: Abstract Intergroup contact interventions often yield limited results in deeply divided societies. We test contact and empathy education in Lebanon, where Syrian refugees comprise a quarter of the population. In a fully cross-randomised field experiment with 887 Lebanese and Syrian youth embedded in a psychosocial support programme, we find that contact has little effect on outgroup attitudes and behaviour, while empathy education consistently improves attitudes for Lebanese youth and behavioural engagement for both. The combined treatment achieves little beyond empathy alone, with no evidence of spillovers to parents (n = 595). In polarised settings, empathy education should precede — or replace — contact.

title: Publication productivity and citation visibility in Turkish gastronomy and culinary arts: a population-level scientometric analysis of academic staff, 2020–2024
Productivity rate metrics for awards and investigators funded by the US National Cancer Institute
abstract: Abstract The proposed scholarly and societal metrics reflect the output efficiency of extramural research funded by the US National Cancer Institute. The productivity of awards or investigators (AoIs) expressed as output COst INdexes (COINs) were calculated based on AoI-linked qualified research articles (qRA) published in single years that follow the AoI-funded years. The outputs for qualified years manifested as either qRA counts or sums of qRA-specific impact values were normalized by the total multi-year amount of funding and, for fractional metrics, by the number of the qRA funders and co-authors. Calculations of the basic (overall) COINs (B-COINs) included all qRAs while translational COINs (T-COINs) were based on a subset of qRAs cited by clinical practice guidelines published by major professional cancer associations. Higher B-COIN values were associated with Early Stage Investigator (ESI) group as compared to non-ESIs. The Outstanding Investigator designation correlated with B-COIN decrease. In multi-component grants, higher B-COINs were observed for the Specialized Programs of Research Excellence (SPORE) project co-leaders (PCLs) funded by SPOREs as compared to performance of the same investigators serving as Principal Investigators (PIs) of other research awards. In contrast, performance of the Program Project Grant (P01) subproject PIs was invariable regardless of the funding source and lower than that of SPORE PCLs supported by SPOREs. The highest T-COINs were associated with awards supporting late phase clinical trials, intermediate values noted for programs focused on early translation (SPOREs), followed by P01 and Research Project Grants (R01). Statistical evidence linked to performance-based metrics may facilitate more efficient investment policies at grant-funding institutions.

title: Evaluating the reliability of web of science citation function classification: evidence from manual annotation and large language models
authors: Lin Zhang; Zhihan Wan; Ming Cheng; Shunshun Shi; Zhenyu Gou
